body:
The Maratha Confederacy in the 18th century

The Marathas emerged as a major political and military force after the decline of Mughal central authority.

During the 18th century, effective leadership of the Maratha state was increasingly exercised by the Peshwa, whose political centre was Pune.

The Maratha political system developed into a confederacy, an association of powerful chiefs who recognised a common political leadership but exercised substantial authority in their own territories.

Important Maratha ruling houses included:

  • Sindhia: Associated with Gwalior and northern Indian territories.
  • Holkar: Associated with Indore and Malwa.
  • Gaekwad: Associated with Baroda in Gujarat.
  • Bhonsle: Associated with Nagpur.

The confederacy possessed considerable military strength but often faced internal disagreements. The British Company exploited these divisions during its expansion.

The Third Battle of Panipat, 1761

The Marathas suffered a major defeat against Ahmad Shah Abdali at the Third Battle of Panipat in 1761.

The defeat weakened Maratha ambitions in northern India but did not immediately destroy Maratha political power. Maratha chiefs remained important regional rulers and continued to confront the East India Company in later decades.

Panipat and the Anglo-Maratha Wars are different conflicts

The Third Battle of Panipat in 1761 was fought between the Marathas and Ahmad Shah Abdali's forces. It was not the Third Anglo-Maratha War. The Third Anglo-Maratha War occurred in 1817–1819.

First Anglo-Maratha War, 1775–1782

The First Anglo-Maratha War developed from disputes over political leadership within the Maratha state and Company intervention in these disputes.

The war ended with the Treaty of Salbai in 1782. Neither side secured a complete military victory, and the settlement provided a period of relative peace between the Company and the Marathas.

The Treaty of Bassein, 1802

The Treaty of Bassein was concluded on 31 December 1802 between the East India Company and Peshwa Baji Rao II.

Facing opposition from rival Maratha leaders, Baji Rao II accepted British military protection and agreed to the stationing of a Company subsidiary force.

The agreement placed major restrictions on the Peshwa's independent political and military authority. Other Maratha chiefs resisted the arrangement because it increased British influence within the confederacy.

Second Anglo-Maratha War, 1803–1805

The Second Anglo-Maratha War followed the Treaty of Bassein and the resistance of important Maratha chiefs to British intervention.

The Company fought Maratha forces on several fronts. The conflict resulted in important British territorial gains, including Delhi, Agra and Orissa, and reduced the power of leading Maratha states.

The capture of Delhi increased British influence over the Mughal emperor, who still possessed considerable symbolic importance despite the decline of Mughal territorial power.

Third Anglo-Maratha War, 1817–1819

The final major Anglo-Maratha conflict began in 1817. British victories during 1817–1818 broke the remaining central power of the Peshwa, while related military operations continued into 1819.

Baji Rao II was removed from power in 1818 and pensioned at Bithur near Kanpur.

The defeat ended the Peshwa's political leadership of the Maratha Confederacy and greatly strengthened British control across central and western India.

The Gujarat connection: Gaekwad of Baroda

The Gaekwad rulers of Baroda were an important Maratha ruling house in Gujarat.

Baroda developed separate political arrangements with the East India Company. In 1802, the Gaekwad government entered into an important subsidiary relationship with the British, involving military assistance and financial obligations.

These arrangements were subsequently consolidated through further agreements, including a treaty in 1805.

The Gaekwad state continued as a princely state under British paramountcy rather than being directly annexed following the defeat of the Peshwa.

This illustrates an important distinction: British defeat of the central Maratha leadership did not mean that every Maratha-ruled territory was absorbed into directly administered Company territory.

Prelims focus

  • 1761: Third Battle of Panipat, Marathas against Ahmad Shah Abdali.
  • 1782: Treaty of Salbai ended the First Anglo-Maratha War.
  • 1802: Treaty of Bassein signed with Peshwa Baji Rao II.
  • 1803–1805: Second Anglo-Maratha War.
  • 1817–1819: Third Anglo-Maratha War; Peshwa Baji Rao II lost power in 1818.
  • Trap: The Treaty of Salbai was signed in 1782; the Treaty of Bassein was signed in 1802.

[Sources: NCERT, Our Pasts–III, Class 8, Chapter 2, From Trade to Territory, p. 18, 2020–21 edition; NCERT, Our Pasts–II, Class 7, Chapter 10, Eighteenth-Century Political Formations, pp. 149–151, 2020–21 edition; Maharashtra State Gazetteer, History, Part III, Chapter 5, discussion of the Treaty of Bassein, p. 116, consulted 20 November 2026; Gazetteer of the Bombay Presidency, History of Gujarat, historical sections on British relations with the Gaekwad and the treaties of 1802 and 1805, consulted 20 November 2026.]

pictures.alt: Timeline separates Panipat from the 3 Anglo-Maratha Wars and shows how Bassein and military defeats reduced the Peshwa’s authority.
pictures.caption: The Maratha political sequence and the 3 wars against the East India Company.

title: The Anglo-Maratha Wars: From the Maratha Confederacy to British Control

body:
Why the Company used political agreements

The East India Company did not acquire every Indian kingdom through direct military conquest. It also used treaties, military assistance and political intervention to increase its influence over Indian rulers.

Such arrangements could allow a ruler to remain on the throne while transferring important military and diplomatic powers to the Company.

The most important arrangement of this kind was the Subsidiary Alliance System, particularly associated with Lord Wellesley, Governor-General from 1798 to 1805.

Meaning of subsidiary alliance

Subsidiary alliance

A subsidiary alliance was an agreement under which an Indian ruler accepted British military protection, maintained or financed British-controlled troops and surrendered substantial independence in external affairs. The ruler generally retained authority over internal administration, subject to increasing British influence.

The main terms commonly associated with the system were:

  • British protection: The Company undertook to provide military protection against external threats and, where agreed, assist the ruler in maintaining his position.
  • Subsidiary troops: The ruler had to maintain or finance a British-controlled military force stationed in or assigned to the state.
  • Financial obligation: The ruler paid for the troops through subsidies, assigned revenues or territorial cessions.
  • Restrictions on foreign relations: Independent treaties, wars and diplomatic relations with other powers were restricted by British control.
  • Military dependence: The ruler's independent military capacity was restricted, although the exact terms differed among treaties and some states retained their own troops.
  • British supervision: Company representatives could exercise substantial political influence over the ruler's decisions.

What happened when payments could not be maintained?

A ruler who failed to meet the financial obligations of a subsidiary alliance could be required to surrender territory or assign additional revenues to the Company.

For example, in 1801 the Nawab of Awadh surrendered substantial territory to the Company in connection with the financial obligations of British protection.

Hyderabad also entered arrangements under which territory was ceded to meet military expenses.

Military protection had a political cost

The Company could present its troops as protection for an Indian ruler while using the same arrangement to restrict the ruler's foreign policy, military independence and financial resources.

British Residents in Indian states

As Company power increased, it appointed political representatives called Residents to Indian courts.

A Resident was a Company representative whose responsibility was to advance British political and commercial interests.

Residents communicated with rulers, supervised political relations and frequently influenced appointments, succession disputes and decisions affecting British interests.

The presence of a Resident did not necessarily mean that the Indian state had been directly annexed. It meant that the Company had acquired an established channel for political intervention.

Examples of subsidiary arrangements

State or rulerImportant yearConnection with the system
Hyderabad1798Important early alliance under Wellesley.
Mysore1799Subsidiary alliance imposed after Tipu Sultan's defeat.
Awadh1801Major territorial cession connected with military obligations.
Baroda1802Gaekwad entered a subsidiary relationship with the Company.
Peshwa Baji Rao II1802Treaty of Bassein accepted British military protection.

These examples demonstrate how subsidiary alliances increased British power in different regions without requiring identical arrangements in every state.

Indirect control and direct annexation

Under indirect control, an Indian ruler remained formally in office but exercised authority within limits imposed by British agreements and supervision.

Under direct annexation, the Company absorbed the territory into its own possessions and replaced the ruler's independent territorial authority.

A subsidiary alliance could weaken a state and make later annexation easier, but the alliance itself was not automatically an annexation.

Prelims focus

  • Lord Wellesley served as Governor-General from 1798 to 1805.
  • The Subsidiary Alliance System is especially associated with Wellesley.
  • 1798: Important subsidiary arrangement with Hyderabad.
  • 1801: Awadh surrendered substantial territory to meet subsidiary military obligations.
  • 1802: Treaty of Bassein brought Peshwa Baji Rao II into a subsidiary relationship.
  • Trap: Accepting a subsidiary alliance did not necessarily mean immediate direct annexation.

[Sources: NCERT, Our Pasts–III, Class 8, Chapter 2, From Trade to Territory, pp. 15–19, 2020–21 edition; Maharashtra State Gazetteer, History, Part III, Chapter 5, Treaty of Bassein, consulted 20 November 2026; Gazetteer of the Bombay Presidency, History of Gujarat, sections on British–Gaekwad agreements of 1802 and 1805, consulted 20 November 2026.]

pictures.alt: The ruler retains the throne and internal administration, while Company protection brings military, diplomatic and financial control.
pictures.caption: The powers retained and surrendered by an Indian ruler under a subsidiary alliance.

title: Subsidiary Alliance and British Residents: Control Without Immediate Annexation

body:
The rise of Sikh political power

The decline of Mughal authority allowed several regional powers to expand, including the Sikhs in Punjab.

During the 18th century, Sikh military groups developed into organisations called misls. These groups controlled territories under different leaders.

Maharaja Ranjit Singh consolidated major Sikh territories and established his capital at Lahore in 1799.

His kingdom became an important political and military power in northwestern India. Its strength limited the eastward expansion of some neighbouring powers and presented a substantial obstacle to British expansion into Punjab.

Punjab under Ranjit Singh

Ranjit Singh developed a strong state supported by military organisation and political consolidation.

The Company established diplomatic relations with his kingdom. The Treaty of Amritsar in 1809 restricted Ranjit Singh's expansion east of the Sutlej, while the British agreed not to interfere in his territories north of the river.

The Company did not annex Ranjit Singh's Punjab kingdom during his lifetime.

He died in 1839. The political instability that followed created conditions for later Anglo-Sikh conflict.

First Anglo-Sikh War, 1845–1846

The First Anglo-Sikh War was fought between the East India Company and the Sikh kingdom.

After major battles, the Sikh forces were defeated. The conflict ended with the Treaty of Lahore in 1846.

The treaty imposed territorial and financial losses on the Sikh kingdom. The Company gained the Jalandhar Doab, the region between the Beas and Sutlej rivers, and substantially increased its political influence over the Lahore government.

However, the Sikh kingdom was not fully annexed in 1846.

Second Anglo-Sikh War, 1848–1849

Further conflict broke out in 1848. The Company fought the Sikh forces in a second major war.

Following British military victories, including the decisive battle of Gujrat in 1849, the Company annexed Punjab in 1849.

The annexation ended the independent political authority of the Sikh kingdom.

The annexation of Sind

British expansion in northwestern India was influenced by commercial, military and strategic concerns, including fears of rival powers approaching India through the northwestern frontier.

The East India Company annexed Sind in 1843, before the Anglo-Sikh Wars.

Punjab was annexed in 1849 after the Second Anglo-Sikh War.

These were distinct territorial acquisitions and should not be grouped under the Doctrine of Lapse.

Distinguish the 2 Anglo-Sikh Wars

The First Anglo-Sikh War ended in 1846 with British influence increasing over the remaining Sikh kingdom. The Second Anglo-Sikh War ended in 1849 with the annexation of Punjab.

Prelims focus

  • 1799: Ranjit Singh established Lahore as his capital.
  • 1809: Treaty of Amritsar with Ranjit Singh.
  • 1839: Death of Maharaja Ranjit Singh.
  • 1845–1846: First Anglo-Sikh War, followed by the Treaty of Lahore.
  • 1848–1849: Second Anglo-Sikh War; Punjab annexed in 1849.
  • Trap: Sind was annexed in 1843, whereas Punjab was annexed in 1849.

[Sources: NCERT, Our Pasts–II, Class 7, Chapter 10, Eighteenth-Century Political Formations, pp. 148–149, 2020–21 edition; NCERT, Our Pasts–III, Class 8, Chapter 2, From Trade to Territory, p. 19, 2020–21 edition; Sikh Museum Initiative, Anglo-Sikh Treaties Project, discussion of the treaties of 1809, 1846 and the annexation settlement of 1849, consulted 20 November 2026.]

pictures.alt: Ranjit Singh's strong kingdom gave way to British dominance after the First Anglo-Sikh War and annexation after the Second; Sind was annexed separately in 1843.

title: The Anglo-Sikh Wars and British Expansion into Punjab and Sind
